title: Boxing and Unboxing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of boxing and unboxing in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply boxing and unboxing to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Boxing and Unboxing is lesson 25 in Variables, Data Types, and Constants. Types define which values an expression can represent and which operations are valid. Make conversions and null handling visible rather than relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: The type system catches many mistakes early, but only when you choose types and conversions deliberately. This lesson focuses on boxing and unboxing and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it

items.title: Understanding boxing
items.text: Boxing converts a value type to an object-compatible representation; unboxing requires the matching runtime value type. Avoid repeated boxing in hot paths when a generic API can preserve the type.

items.title: Understanding unboxing
items.text: Boxing converts a value type to an object-compatible representation; unboxing requires the matching runtime value type. Avoid repeated boxing in hot paths when a generic API can preserve the type.

items.title: Value types stored as objects
items.text: A value-type assignment copies the value; copying a reference-type variable copies the reference, so both variables may refer to the same object. Test with a small before/after example to see which state is shared.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates boxing and unboxing. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates boxing and unboxing rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for boxing and unboxing before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.
